Currently, whoaverse may be seen by new users as a rather unwelcoming community, with strict voting system. When new users try to vote on something, they are greeted with a message explaining that they can not vote unless they get a few positive comment points (CCP).

Many people are lurkers and only like to engage in voting, which is still helpful as these users with their votes help liven up the community. They are referred to as "the warriors of /v/all/new", they dig in and vote on content which would otherwise remain unnoticed and bring it to our attention.

So, I started working on a new system which can be configured and tuned until we have the best effect. In essence, new users can be given a fixed set of votes to use during a 24 hour period, even if they don't have any CCP or LCP whatsoever. To begin with, they will be given 10 votes each 24 hours (unused votes are lost). This should be enough for many lurkers, but if they want to get more votes, they will need to engage in submitting links, starting discussions or posting comments.

I would like to hear community input on this as it is rolled out (I will post an update when this system is live).

Update: this new system is now active and in place. New users can now upvote up to 10 submissions or comments (combined) in a 24 hour period. They are unable to downvote unless they have at least 100 CCP. Please report any bugs you may discover with this new change. Thank you! :)
Towards a more friendly welcome for new users
.. I was thinking we should call them "Eyes of All", it has a nice ring to it, but isn't like Reddit's "Knights of New".

I honestly have to say that I feel this makes matters worse. People want to contribute to a community right away, in a way that they feel comfortable or have fun contributing. There's nothing wrong with upvotes, people should be able to "spread the love" all they want. These requirements / restrictions should apply only to downvotes, and will there-by help reduce vote-brigading and trolling. Not to upvotes, where they serve only to restrict users who want to "help" as well as discouraging participation (or returning!)

When I learned that a post has to have someone upvote it before it can be seen in "hot," I immediately went "Knight of New" and started upvoting every post that tickled my fancy. I can honestly say that in that moment if I had run out of upvotes to give these poor unseen contributions to the site, that I would have shuffled on off to Facebook again, where I can "like" anything I feel like liking. I may not have been back.

I have to agree, this discourages participatiion more than it encourages it, and endagers return user counts.

The ranking system IMO, is flawed at the moment. 2 votes and you get into "Hot"? That isn't hot, that is something that got upvoted once. It could be anything, it could be far from "hot" or "popular". It should take considerable (greater than avg. comparison or reference number) power for something to be thrust into "Hot".

A submission about reptilian aliens in the White House that got upvoted by 1 other person within 5 minutes of it's submission isn't "Hot" and shouldn't be on top of submissions that have accumulated 2x to 5x the number of votes on the front page or All. It doesn't make sense.

While I agree with you that the ranking system is flawed, I'm actually of the exact opposite opinion on how it should be. Anything posted should have it's place in Hot. Think of hot not as "everything in this list is hot," but (as was intended) "This list is sorted by how "hot" submissions currently are." As it is, over there on that other place submissions submitted will go overlooked just because anything new is as far down the list as #100 when first submitted (on that own sub's list... you'll never even see it when using front or all). I feel that eventually Whoaverse should do it just the same, not requiring approval by "elitists" or "power-users" (i.e.: those who even know about this "rule" for how things happen) for submissions to be put into the "main stream" of the site. This is, though I'm sure they don't realize it, actually a form of censorship.

That being said, I actually wouldn't suggest changing it right now. (DEFINITELY not to increase the # required!) While the site is small, this acts as another layer of defense against spammers and trolls, and (at this point at least) it's benefit outweighs it's drawback.

As it is, over there on that other place submissions submitted will go overlooked just because anything new is as far down the list as #100 when first submitted (on that own sub's list... you'll never even see it when using front or all).

Then how do those submissions that are ranked 1, 2 ... 10 or whatever even get there in the first place? They were new at some point too. Clearly people do look at new submissions. Not everybody may look at them (for instance on /v/all or /r/all if we're talking about reddit,) but there are enough people that do to keep the front page and "hot" pages from being stagnant.

If you're saying that the "new" tab is only perused by "power users" then frankly the problem is with the entire voting model in general where submissions are forced to compete with one another and are subject to the flaws of democracy (especially when you say it's a form of censorship.)

Once you get into that discussion then it brings out everything that MarkW keeps talking about- controls on submissions, possibly controls on votes, etc. It's a tired discussion for me so I don't even want to go there.

To make it better I'd just propose having the "Rising" tab that reddit has so that people can see what's new and rising. Because a fresh submission with 1 or 2 votes (or in relative terms, maybe 10% of the average votes in "Hot") is exactly that- a "rising" submission. Whereas "Hot" is what it implies- something that is popular with the users and have been demonstrated as such with a high vote count.

The other way would be to make "New" the "default" page a user lands on, but that defeats the entire point of having a community filter out the very best submissions and you'd have an ecletic mix of the shitty and the good out front for everyone to see.

There may be something that you overlooked. As I understand it, the restriction is there so to make it difficult for someone to register 10+ accounts for the purposes of "astro-turfing" or otherwise manipulating votes.

Also, the manipulation isn't neccessary done with downvotes... I can easily push something down by upvoting every other submission but the target submission. This will effectively push it down by lifting everything else up.

The 100 karma threshold is there as a sort of proof of work. This is actually a step back by enabling new users a certain number of votes. It is one that I am okay with, but diminishes the effectiveness of the system.

Not to upvotes, where they serve only to restrict users who want to "help" as well as discouraging participation (or returning!)

What I want to know, and especially seeing that the site is in Alpha and open to experimentation, is whether the data indicates an increase in user activity given the new regime or no increase. If there is an increase, then how much? Then you can tailor or optimize the limit.
